# Part 1 Project Configuration

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)      
library(dplyr)        
library(tidyr)       
library(ggplot2)      
library(broom.mixed) 
library(performance)  
library(gt)           
library(readr)       
library(DHARMa)       
library(ggeffects)    
library(titanic)      

titanic <- titanic_train                     

titanic <- titanic |>                        
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>      
  drop_na() |>                              
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(                  
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,                     
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>               
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(               
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(                 
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>  
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)  

n <- nrow(titanic)                          
```

Female passengers had a much higher survival rate than male passengers
(75.5% compared with 20.5%). Survival rates also declined with ticket
class: first-class passengers had the highest survival rate, followed by
second-class and then third-class passengers. These patterns are
consistent with my expectations, as women and passengers in higher
ticket classes may have been given priority during the evacuation.

```{r}
age_desc |>
```

```{r}
surv_sex <- titanic |>
```

# Part 2 Specify competing binary logistic regression

I expect all three predictors to be related to survival. First, I expect
female passengers to be more likely to survive than male passengers. In
1912, people often followed the rule of "women and children first," so
women may have had better access to the lifeboats. Second, I expect
passengers in higher ticket classes to be more likely to survive.
First-class passengers may have had cabins closer to the lifeboats and
may have received more help from the crew. Third, I expect younger
passengers to be more likely to survive than older passengers, because
children may also have been given priority during the evacuation.

```{r}
mod0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1, data = titanic,       
                family = binomial(link = "logit"))                

mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex,                                   
  data = titanic,                                   
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass,                         
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age,                    
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

```

In each model, the intercept is the log-odds of survival for the
reference group, that is, when every predictor is at its reference
category or equals zero. In mod1, the intercept is the log-odds of
survival for female passengers, because female is the reference category
for Sex. In mod2, the intercept becomes the log-odds of survival for
female passengers in first class, because first class is the reference
category for Pclass. In mod3, the intercept is the log-odds of survival
for a female, first-class passenger who is 0 years old. Since no
passenger in the data is exactly 0 years old, the mod3 intercept is not
very meaningful on its own.

# Part 3 Compare model performance

The full model (mod3) provides the best fit to the data, with the lowest
AIC (657.28) and the lowest BIC (680.14) of the four models. Both
indices penalize model complexity, so these values indicate that mod3
offers the best balance of fit and complexity. Both AIC and BIC
decreased with each added predictor, although the decrease became
smaller at each step: AIC fell by about 212 with the addition of sex, 74
with ticket class, and 23 with age. The likelihood-ratio tests showed
that each addition significantly improved model fit (all ps \< .001).
Sex produced the largest improvement, χ²(1) = 213.82, followed by ticket
class, χ²(2) = 78.27, and age, χ²(1) = 25.15. AIC, BIC, and the
likelihood-ratio tests therefore support the same conclusion.

```{r}
# 3.1 Nested-model chi-square tests 
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)   

tests <- tests |>
  select(Chisq, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>      
  rename(
    Nested.df = `Chi Df`,                       
    Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,                 
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`)             

# 3.2 Extract model-level performance 
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod0)   
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod1)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod3)

#  combine model metrics
mods <- c(                             
  "mod0: Null",
  "mod1: Sex",
  "mod2: + Pclass",
  "mod3: + Age")

glances <- rbind(                      
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3)

# 3.3 Combine nested tests and model performance 
comparison_table <- cbind(             
  Model = mods,                       
  glances,                             
  tests)                              

# model comparison table
comparison_table |>
  select(                              
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>                              
  cols_label(                         
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(                          
    columns = c(
      AIC,
      BIC,
      logLik,
      deviance,
      Nested.Chisq.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(                                 
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),                      
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))  
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(                         
    columns = c(Nested.df, Nested.Chisq.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

# Additional performance comparison 
performance_comparison <- compare_performance( 
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3,
  rank = TRUE)                                  
```

# Part 4 Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

```{r}
# chunk: select model
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>       
  slice_tail(n = 1)                     

#creating an object with our selected model's name for dynamic reporting
selected_name <- selected_row$Model     

#case matching for dynamic reporting
selected_model <- switch(               
  selected_name,
  "mod0: Null" = mod0,
  "mod1: Sex" = mod1,
  "mod2: + Pclass" = mod2,
  "mod3: + Age" = mod3)

# 4.1a dharma sim
set.seed(9041)                                    
res_sel <- simulateResiduals(selected_model,       
                             n = 500,              
                             plot = FALSE)         

#  dharma plot
plot(res_sel)   

# 4.1b vif, vif plot
vif_plot <- plot(check_collinearity(selected_model))  
vif_plot                                        

# 4.1c Complete separation

# 4.1d Influential observations outliers)
outlier_test <- testOutliers(res_sel, plot = FALSE)     

# 4.1e Events per predictor 
n_event <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)               
n_nonevent <- sum(titanic$Survived == 0)            
n_coef <- length(fixef(selected_model)$cond)     
```

The diagnostics suggest that mod3 fits the data well. First, the DHARMa
residuals showed no distributional misfit, with non-significant
uniformity (p = .903), dispersion (p = .812), and outlier tests (p =
.541). Second, all VIFs were below 1.5. Third, there was no sign of
complete separation, because every cell contained both outcomes and
fitted probabilities ranged from .017 to .976. Fourth, the 290 survivors
provide 58 events per coefficient, above the rule of 10. The only
potential problem is a slight U-shape in the residual-versus-predicted
plot, although the combined quantile test was non-significant. This
pattern may reflect a non-linear age effect or an unmodelled
interaction. Thus, the direction and significance of the associations
appear trustworthy, but the age odds ratio is best read as an average
linear trend.

# Part 5 selecting a model

```{r}
# 5.2 Extract coefficients with tidy()

coefficient_results <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  selected_model,
  effects = "fixed",          
  component = "cond",         
  conf.int = TRUE,            
  conf.level = 0.95) |>       
  mutate(
    odds.ratio = exp(estimate),   # log-odds -> odds ratio
    or.low     = exp(conf.low),   # lower CI limit as odds ratio
    or.high    = exp(conf.high))  # upper CI limit as odds ratio
```
I selected the full model (mod3), which includes sex, ticket class, and age, as my preferred model. First, the nested-model χ²-tests showed that each added predictor significantly improved model fit, including age, χ²(1) = 25.15, p < .001. Second, mod3 had the lowest AIC (657.28) and the lowest BIC (680.14) of the four models. Because BIC applies a strong penalty for complexity, this result shows that the extra predictors are worth including. Third, mod3 is still a simple model with only five coefficients, and the 290 survivors provide enough events to estimate them. Fourth, the diagnostics showed no serious problems: the DHARMa tests were non-significant, collinearity was low, and there was no complete separation. Finally, mod3 is easy to interpret and directly tests all three of my predictions. 

```{r}
# Coefficient table

coefficient_results |>
  select(
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI upper",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      estimate,
      std.error,
      conf.low,
      conf.high
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        x < .001,
        "< .001",
        sprintf("%.3f", x)
      )
    }
  )

# Log-odds coefficients

b_male <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Sexmale") |> pull(estimate)  # Sexmale log-odds
b_p2   <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass2") |> pull(estimate)  # Pclass2 log-odds
b_p3   <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass3") |> pull(estimate)  # Pclass3 log-odds
b_age  <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Age")     |> pull(estimate)  # Age log-odds

# Odds ratios and their 95% CIs
or_male  <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Sexmale") |> pull(odds.ratio)
or_male_l <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Sexmale") |> pull(or.low)
or_male_h <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Sexmale") |> pull(or.high)

or_p2   <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass2") |> pull(odds.ratio)
or_p2_l <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass2") |> pull(or.low)
or_p2_h <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass2") |> pull(or.high)

or_p3   <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass3") |> pull(odds.ratio)
or_p3_l <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass3") |> pull(or.low)
or_p3_h <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Pclass3") |> pull(or.high)

or_age   <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Age") |> pull(odds.ratio)
or_age_l <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Age") |> pull(or.low)
or_age_h <- coefficient_results |> filter(term == "Age") |> pull(or.high)

coefs <- tidy(mod3, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(effect == "fixed") |>
  mutate(OR = exp(estimate), OR.low = exp(conf.low), OR.high = exp(conf.high))

sex <- coefs |> filter(term == "Sexmale")
c2  <- coefs |> filter(term == "Pclass2")
c3  <- coefs |> filter(term == "Pclass3")
age <- coefs |> filter(term == "Age")

r2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p)))


```

Holding ticket class and age constant, male passengers had lower log-odds of survival than female passengers (b = `r r2(sex$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r r2(sex$conf.low)`, `r r2(sex$conf.high)`], p `r fmt_p(sex$p.value)`). In other words, the odds of survival for male passengers were `r r2(sex$OR)` times the odds for female passengers (OR 95% CI [`r r2(sex$OR.low)`, `r r2(sex$OR.high)`]). 

Holding sex and age constant, second-class passengers had lower log-odds of survival than first-class passengers (b = `r r2(c2$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r r2(c2$conf.low)`, `r r2(c2$conf.high)`], p `r fmt_p(c2$p.value)`), so their odds of survival were `r r2(c2$OR)` times the odds of first-class passengers (OR 95% CI [`r r2(c2$OR.low)`, `r r2(c2$OR.high)`]). 

Third-class passengers had even lower log-odds of survival than first-class passengers (b = `r r2(c3$estimate)`, 95% CI [`r r2(c3$conf.low)`, `r r2(c3$conf.high)`], p `r fmt_p(c3$p.value)`), and their odds of survival were `r r2(c3$OR)` times the odds of first-class passengers (OR 95% CI [`r r2(c3$OR.low)`, `r r2(c3$OR.high)`]). 

Finally, holding sex and ticket class constant, each one-year increase in age changed the log-odds of survival by `r r2(age$estimate)` (95% CI [`r r2(age$conf.low)`, `r r2(age$conf.high)`], p `r fmt_p(age$p.value)`). This means that each additional year of age multiplied the odds of survival by `r r2(age$OR)` (OR 95% CI [`r r2(age$OR.low)`, `r r2(age$OR.high)`]), which is about a `r round((1 - age$OR) * 100, 1)`% decrease in the odds per year.

```{r}
    AIC,

    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual df",
    Nested.df = "Nested df",
    Nested.Chisq.stat = "Nested χ²",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = where(is.numeric),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
  )
```

In this analysis, I used binary logistic regression to examine whether sex, ticket class, and age were associated with surviving the Titanic crash among `r n` passengers. I compared four nested models, starting with an intercept-only model and adding sex, ticket class, and age one at a time. The full model (mod3) had the lowest AIC and BIC, and each added predictor significantly improved model fit. I therefore selected mod3 as my preferred model. In this model, sex was the strongest predictor of survival. Holding ticket class and age constant, the odds of survival for male passengers were `r r2(sex$OR)` times the odds for female passengers (95% CI [`r r2(sex$OR.low)`, `r r2(sex$OR.high)`]). Ticket class also mattered. Compared with first-class passengers, the odds of survival were `r r2(c2$OR)` times as high for second-class passengers (95% CI [`r r2(c2$OR.low)`, `r r2(c2$OR.high)`]) and `r r2(c3$OR)` times as high for third-class passengers (95% CI [`r r2(c3$OR.low)`, `r r2(c3$OR.high)`]). Finally, each additional year of age multiplied the odds of survival by `r r2(age$OR)` (95% CI [`r r2(age$OR.low)`, `r r2(age$OR.high)`]). Thus, the results support all three of my predictions: female, higher-class, and younger passengers were more likely to survive.

```{r}
# 5.6 Visualize one predictor with ggpredict()
# other predictors held at reference/typical values
pred_age <- ggpredict(selected_model, terms = "Age [0:80 by=1]")

ggplot(pred_age, aes(x, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Survival"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```


# Part 6: Discuss your findings and limitations

The results suggest that sex was the most important predictor of survival, followed by ticket class and then age. Adding sex to the null model produced by far the largest improvement in fit, χ²(1) = 213.82, compared with χ²(2) = 78.27 for ticket class and χ²(1) = 25.15 for age. This pattern fits the "women and children first" rule, which gave women the clearest advantage in reaching the lifeboats. Ticket class also mattered a great deal, even after sex and age were held constant. This suggests that socioeconomic status shaped who survived, possibly because first-class cabins were closer to the lifeboats. Age had the smallest effect, but older passengers were still less likely to survive. Thus, survival on the Titanic seems to have depended mostly on who a passenger was (sex) and partly on what they could afford (ticket class).

This analysis has several limitations. First, the sample includes only the 714 passengers with complete age data, so the results may not represent all passengers on board. Second, the model treats age as a straight-line effect, but the slight U-shape in the residual plot suggests that the age effect may not be linear. For example, children may have had a clear advantage that a single slope cannot fully capture.
